author: Tertullian
addressee: Christians, especially newcomers beginning to hear divine teaching
occasion: Tertullian writes to instruct Christians on the true nature and discipline of repentance, correcting pagan misunderstandings and warning against presumption that delays or cheapens repentance.
argument: Repentance is a discipline ordained by God and must be directed only toward sins, never toward good deeds. Those who undertake repentance must not return to sin, since doing so insults God and exalts the devil. Newcomers must not presume on coming forgiveness by delaying repentance. For those who sin after baptism, God grants one further repentance, which must be carried out through exomologesis, a public discipline of confession and humiliation that restores the sinner to God.

outline.move: Tertullian describes how people without knowledge of God misunderstand repentance, even regretting their own good deeds.
He argues that repentance has a rational form given by God, serves human salvation, and must never be applied to good deeds.
He distinguishes sins of body and spirit, act and will, showing that even unfulfilled evil desires require repentance.
He urges sinners to embrace repentance as God's command and promise of life.
He warns that repentance once undertaken must not be undone by returning to sin, which would insult God and exalt the devil.
He rebukes newcomers who presume on coming forgiveness and delay true repentance.
He introduces the possibility of a second repentance after baptism, granted once only, and urges gratitude rather than abuse.
He proves from Scripture and the parables of the lost sheep, coin, and prodigal son that God welcomes the repentant sinner.
He describes exomologesis, the outward discipline of confession, fasting, mourning, and prostration that accompanies true repentance.
He answers the objection of shame, arguing that public confession before the church is Christ himself and brings healing.
He contrasts the luxury of the unrepentant with the self-denial of the penitent, and shames Christians by comparison with pagan office-seekers.
He urges repentance by the terrors of hell and the examples of the deer, the swallow, Nebuchadnezzar, Pharaoh, and Adam.

cast.name: Tertullian
cast.who: The author, a Christian teacher addressing the church.

cast.name: John the Baptist
cast.who: The prophet who preached repentance before the Lord's coming.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first human, whose sin brought condemnation, and who was restored by exomologesis.

cast.name: Nebuchadnezzar
cast.who: The Babylonian king restored after seven years of penitential humiliation.

cast.name: Pharaoh
cast.who: The Egyptian ruler who rejected repentance and perished in the sea.

voices.speaker: John the Baptist
voices.how_marked: direct quotation introduced by 'Non tacet Ioannes'

voices.speaker: An imagined objector
voices.how_marked: rhetorical questions and objections introduced by 'sed aiunt quidam' and similar phrases

key_terms.sense: Repentance, the divinely appointed discipline of turning from sin and seeking God's forgiveness
The public discipline of confession and humiliation by which a sinner seeks restoration after baptism
Baptism, the washing that seals faith and grants forgiveness of sins
Those preparing for baptism, still under instruction in the faith
The one further repentance available after baptism for post-baptismal sins
Forgiveness of sins, granted by God through repentance and baptism
Salvation, the goal of repentance and the gift of God's mercy
Fear of God, the beginning of repentance and safeguard against sin
Sin, an offense against God, whether in act or will
Presumption on God's forgiveness, treating baptism or repentance as a license to sin
Defiant disobedience, the attitude of one who returns to sin after knowing God
The making of amends to God through confession and penitential discipline
Hell, the eternal fire that threatens the unrepentant
The baptismal washing, the seal of faith

scripture: Tertullian uses the Old Latin version, which follows the Septuagint for book names and Psalm numbering. He refers to the churches addressed in Revelation (Ephesus, Thyatira, Sardis, Pergamum, Laodicea) and to the parables of the lost sheep, lost coin, and prodigal son. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and Psalm numbering (e.g., LXX Psalm 50 = Psalm 51 in modern numbering).
uncertain: The exact date of composition; c. 203 is a common estimate but not certain.
Whether Tertullian wrote this before or after his turn to Montanism; the work is generally placed before it.
The precise identity of the 'hearers' (audientes) as a formal catechumenate class in Carthage at this time.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Paenitentiam hoc genus hominum, quod et ipsi retro fuimus, caeci, sine domini lumine, natura tenus norunt
_unresolved_facts.fix: Tertullian describes people without knowledge of God ("sine domini lumine"), not specifically pagans; he includes himself and all who were formerly without God's light. The target is broader than 'pagan misunderstandings'—it's anyone lacking divine reason.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Adam... who was restored by exomologesis
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: quam ipse quoque et stirpis humanae et offensae in dominum princeps Adam, exomologesi restitutus in paradisum suum, non tacet
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source does say Adam was restored by exomologesis, but this is a highly unusual claim not found in Genesis or standard Christian tradition. The brief should flag this as Tertullian's unique interpretation rather than present it straightforwardly.

_unresolved_facts.claim: God... direct quotation introduced by 'dicens' or 'inquit'... sections: ["4"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: dicens ad populum, Paenitere, et salvum faciam te. Et iterum, Vivo, inquit, dominus, et paenitentiam malo quiam mortem
_unresolved_facts.fix: God speaks in sections 2 and 4, not just 4. In section 2: "Paenitentiam initote, dicens, iam enim salus nationibus appropinquabit" (through John the Baptist's preaching, but as divine command); and the extended divine speech about God's own repentance and plan. The brief underrepresents God's voice.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Non tacet Ioannes, Paenitentiam initote, dicens, iam enim salus nationibus appropinquabit, dominus scilicet, afferens secundum dei promissum
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source does not mark John with direct quotation introduced by 'Non tacet Ioannes' as a voice marker in the way described. Tertullian reports John's preaching content; it's not a direct quotation marked as speech. The 'dicens' attaches to God's message through John, not John's own speaking voice.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Sed aiunt quidam satis deum habere, si corde et animo suspiciatur
_unresolved_facts.fix: The objector appears in section 5, but sections 6 and 10 do not contain 'sed aiunt quidam' or similar objection formulas. Section 6 has rhetorical questions but no marked objector voice. Section 10 addresses 'plerique' (many) who avoid exomologesis out of shame—this is descriptive, not an objector voice. Correct to ["5"] only, or note section 10's different construction.

The source says 'Sardos' not 'Sardians'—the brief uses a different form. More importantly, the source says they are accused of 'non plenorum operum' (incomplete works), which the brief omits. The name mapping is incomplete.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Collocavit in vestibulo paenitentiam secundam, quae pulsantibus patefaciat; sed iam semel, quia iam secundo; sed amplius nunquam, quia proxime frustra
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says 'iam semel, quia iam secundo'—'now once, because already a second time'—meaning this second repentance is granted once (not to be repeated), not that it is 'granted once only' in an absolute sense. The phrasing 'granted once only' could mislead; it's 'one more time, never again after that.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["12"]: 'the deer, the swallow, Nebuchadnezzar, Pharaoh, and Adam'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Cervus sagitta transfixus... Hirundo, si excaecaverit pullos... Peccator restituendo sibi institutam a domino exomologesin sciens praeteribit illam, quae Babylonium regem in regna restituit?... Aegyptius imperator... Adam, exomologesi restitutus in paradisum suum
_unresolved_facts.fix: The deer and swallow are not examples of repentance but of animals knowing their natural remedies. Tertullian uses them as analogies for humans who should recognize their spiritual medicine (exomologesis). The brief conflates analogical examples with actual repentant figures. The structure should distinguish: animals as analogies, then human exempla of repentance (Nebuchadnezzar) and its rejection (Pharaoh), plus Adam.
